sm: The host introduces Harmeet Dhillon, the former head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, who left after about nineteen months and was then attacked by parts of the new right. Asked why, she says the Trump era brought in a helpful new coalition, including Indian, Hispanic and black voters, and that winning requires coalition building rather than gatekeeping. She blames paid promotion on social media and podcasts for a race to the bottom that gives permission to hateful, isolationist views. She says people she once worked with, including Tucker Carlson, now wink at anti-Semitism and racism.

Dhillon says she was limited in what she could say while in government, and now that she has left she is free to speak. She urges the Republican Party to sober up, saying the 2026 election result was partly due to its failure to police its own rhetoric. She says she would never appear at an event featuring Nick Fuentes, and notes she sees foreign influence boosting hateful online speech. The host adds that bots and paid influencers can fake social proof, which then becomes real, and says no one in government is acting on it.

Dhillon says she has long called for reform of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, arguing it now shields platforms that manipulate algorithms, which she calls the companies' own content. She describes losing cases against Twitter over banned conservatives, including a feminist writer, because courts said platforms can do as they like. The host argues regulation is justified so no single company is disadvantaged by removing bots first. Dhillon agrees, says no one now talks about censorship because bigotry is allowed to run free, and suspects China or Middle Eastern money paid for divisive messaging in the election.

The host asks whether dissident voices should be engaged and how, given Tucker Carlson's interview with Nick Fuentes. Dhillon says she has known Carlson since her early twenties, is sad to see his evolution, and thinks it is fine to talk with fringe figures only if they are tested rather than validated. She compares this to the Federalist Society, which hosts debates and panels. She says she held back criticism while in government because the White House tightly controlled what she said. The host admits personal loyalty also made him slow to criticize friends in the movement, such as Candace Owens.

The host says that as CEO he defended his colleagues like a bulldog, and that loyalty kept him quiet too long about Candace Owens. Dhillon says she was always suspicious of Owens because of her pro-Obama past and viewed her as toxic from the start. She recounts that when Attorney General Pam Bondi came under bot-driven attack over the Epstein files, Charlie Kirk and Megyn Kelly criticized Bondi at a Turning Point event in Tampa and suggested Dhillon replace her. She told them privately it was unfair, refused to speak at the conference, and Turning Point never invited her back.

Dhillon says Charlie Kirk came to her office a few months later, said he had apologized to Pam Bondi, and they made up, weeks before he was assassinated. She says doing the right thing cost her relationships, and that top conservatives are not defending her because they fear losing their anti-immigrant base. The host says young men swung toward Democrats in the midterms. He argues pandemic lockdowns pushed young men online, but says the movement has spread to mainstream churches, rooted in real economic strain and a narrative that young white men are blamed for every ill.

The host explains that some young men reject the idea of a propositional nation. He says America was founded on ideas but by a particular, largely English Protestant people, and that these young men blame immigrants and successful minorities for their hardship. He asks how conservatives can answer these concerns without pandering to racist, anti-Semitic fervor. Dhillon says every generation clashes with the last, and her concern is conservative politicians who echo these themes, whether through consultants or AI. She says criticizing the war is not anti-Semitic but blaming Jews for everything is, and she is shocked to see Indian immigrants called frauds.

Dhillon describes growing up in rural North Carolina, where her father was a country doctor. She says immigrant doctors have served nearly everyone, yet resentment is rising and too few politicians push back. She defends giving the prayer at the Republican National Convention as outreach, says Republicans cannot win with only the white Christian vote, and says saying heritage American really means white. She criticizes the attack on Hindu-looking and brown teenagers, saying pastors spreading racist rhetoric give permission for it. She calls anti-Semitism evil and recalls telling Harvard students that Harvard's DEI roots lie in capping Jewish admissions.

Asked whether a country can choose its immigrants, Dhillon says yes. She describes her Civil Rights Division work treating preference for temporary visa workers over Americans as national origin discrimination, winning tens of millions of dollars in settlements. She would fix H-1B by requiring pay fifty percent above prevailing wage, and says India has improved so fewer want to leave. She opposes loose refugee claims, says Sharia law and loudspeaker calls to prayer are problematic, and says both parties rely on cheap, often illegal labor, citing California wineries.

The host says America was once called a melting pot, but the left replaced that with multiculturalism, and asks whether the country is now seen as merely an economic zone. Dhillon notes the melting pot talk now comes from the right and that assimilation should not mean changing religion. She recalls a Ku Klux Klan welcome sign in her North Carolina town, yet says people treated her family kindly, and her brother is a famous Duke basketball fan in a turban. She says most immigrants embrace American culture but some refugee enclaves resist it, and she opposes adding holidays.

Asked whether some religious traditions can be barred from immigration, the host raises Sharia as a thought that exploits pluralism. Dhillon describes her family's Punjab history and the partition, and says she knows many Muslims who do not support Sharia, and many Muslims voted for Trump. She would not generalize, but supports tests of viewpoint, such as rejecting communism and requiring respect for religious liberty and equality for women, and denaturalization for those who lied. The host then raises pastor Joel Webbon, who says his group does not need democracy or a majority.

The host says Webbon's group plans to deport a hundred million people and make the country white and Christian. He argues the new right sees politics as raw power and redefines freedom as the freedom to behave virtuously, and that some figures in the administration share this outlook. Dhillon says she was privy to top-level conversations but cannot name names, perhaps in a future book. She says the Reagan tradition of a tolerant, pluralistic party is still her party, that the stewards of the Republican National Committee are decent, and that corrupt consultants worsen the problem.

Dhillon says consultants may chase dollars and pander to the worst elements, and that few in the administration truly dislike immigrants, mostly online. She says there is no Groyper presence at the Justice Department, and that other agencies have some among men in their twenties. The host argues the root problem is incentives, since people follow what is in vogue, and asks how to fix it. Dhillon says all is not lost, praising a Marco Rubio speech at the Federalist Society about Americans by choice, and says donors have power and should insist on discipline in the party.

Dhillon says donors may be waking up, and that Victor Davis Hanson called out former friends. She urges people to vote with their feet, since listening to toxic shows generates revenue for the hosts. She stresses moral courage, church attendance, faith, and homeschooling. The host says anti-Semitism arrived in America quickly and so could fade as quickly, like a fad. Dhillon adds that she made going after anti-Semitism and anti-Christian bias a focus of the Civil Rights Division, with prompt investigations of firebombings of churches and synagogues.

Dhillon says houses of worship are under attack from secularism and Marxism, and links the trans movement to nihilism, citing a book on the Zizians and claiming many shooters are trans. She says every attack on a house of worship was prosecuted as a hate crime, including a case against Don Lemon and others over a church disruption in St. Paul. She describes investigating over a hundred universities for DEI and anti-Semitism, including Harvard and Columbia, with settlements. She also cites creating a Second Amendment section and suing California, Colorado, Virginia and Washington, D.C.

Dhillon describes enforcing parental rights laws, FERPA and PPRA, against schools hiding gender changes from parents. She says she reopened the Protecting American Workers initiative, winning settlements over fake job advertising used to sponsor green cards, with a large case against Microsoft. She says she also fought race-based city programs, reparations, and DEI hiring. She says about three hundred of four hundred lawyers left the division, which she calls a signature accomplishment, and that she then hired over a hundred thirty new people.

Dhillon explains that she ended dozens of consent decrees on police departments and schools, which she says burdened cities with costly monitors and drove good officers away. She says the school decrees dated back decades, calls this the reverse Sherman's March, and says the NAACP mostly failed in court to stop her. She says becoming Attorney General was never her ambition and she did not leave over being passed over. She missed private practice, where she could litigate First Amendment cases, disliked living in D.C., and would consider future service.

Dhillon says she is returning to rebuild her law firm and may write a book or advise companies on DEI. She says the president did not ask her to resign. She told chief of staff Susie Wiles on October thirteenth that she intended to leave, and the 60 Minutes interview came days later at the White House's request. She says she posted the two aired clips, which said the Justice Department will not send troops to the polls and was sending a thousand monitors, and that Trump never criticized her over it. She blames DC leaks.

Dhillon expects Democratic oversight and subpoenas, says she will comply with legal obligations, has lawyers offering to represent her, and previously helped represent Pam Bondi. She argues Democratic committee time spent harassing officials may slow their agenda. The host asks about her Sikh faith. She explains that Sikhism began in the 1600s in India, that its first guru rejected the caste system and taught equality, and that there are fewer than thirty million Sikhs. She notes its 1,400-page holy book and the tradition of defending the defenseless against forced conversions.

Dhillon continues explaining Sikhism: the tenth guru took up arms against forced conversion, baptized Sikhs wear a dagger, and men and women are equal. Sikhs live as householders, practice charity and respect other faiths, and do not proselytize. Each temple has the Guru Granth Sahib and a free vegetarian kitchen. She says she felt comfortable praying with fellow Republican National Committee members, and trusts people of faith more than secular people. She cites going to the Supreme Court three times during COVID for Christian worship rights. The host thanks her and says he looks forward to her speaking from the outside.
